title: 21. Thirty days from beginner to useful
heading: Thirty days from beginner to useful
label: Study plan
summary: A day-by-day month through the guide, with a calculation or a primary document every day, a way of reading any article on this market, questions to ask each kind of practitioner, and a final week that ends in choosing something to contribute.

spans.text: This plan takes a reader with no background in hardware or finance through the whole guide in thirty days, at about an hour on weekdays and a longer session at each weekend. It aims at three abilities. To read any article on this market and say what it measures, what it assumes, and what its author sells. To hold a conversation with someone who builds, finances, or trades compute, and ask the question that shows where their knowledge ends. And to see which unanswered question you are unusually well placed to work on.
Every day has something to read and something to do. The doing matters more. A number you have recomputed stays with you; a number you have read does not.

Before each session, open the dashboard and write three numbers in a notebook with the date: the marketplace asking price of an H100, the cheapest output price for one open-weight model of your choice, and the high-yield credit spread. It takes two minutes. By day thirty you will have your own series for a rental price, a token price, and a credit price, and you will have seen for yourself which of them moves, which is sticky, and whether they move together. That is the beginning of judgment about this market, and it cannot be got from reading.

blocks.text: How to read any article on this market

spans.text: Apply the same seven questions to everything, including this guide.

items.text: Who wrote it, and what do they sell?

An inference provider wants cheap hardware finance. A firm building a clearinghouse concludes that a clearinghouse is missing. That does not make either wrong; it tells you which claims to check first.
Which market?
The strategic market of two labs and four hyperscalers, or the open market for inference. Most confusion comes from an argument about one being applied to the other.
Which price?
A rental price has a chip, a contract length, and a venue. A token price is one of three, from one provider. A credit price has a borrower and a term.
What is the denominator?
Per hour or per year. Per accelerator or per megawatt. Contract value over five years or revenue over one.
What kind of statement is it?
A definition, a measurement, an estimate, or a scenario, in the sense of
Chapter 1
Which rung of evidence?
A model, a quote, or a print, in the sense of
Chapter 9
What would show it to be wrong?
If nothing would, it is not yet a claim.

spans.text: By the end of the week you can explain why a profitable company can have negative free cash flow, why a lender wants a three-year contract before it will fund a cluster, why the customer's prepayment ends up as the operator's equity, and why a trusted resale price would be worth more than a better interest rate.
The goal is to read a price, say what it carries, and draw an inference from two prices that neither gives alone. This week uses the observatory's data directly.

rows.text: On the dashboard's quote ladder, choose a model and find the output ratio at which the cheapest-ranked endpoint stops being cheaper than the builder. Revisit your day-11 guess about who is paid.

Rebuild the price stack from a megawatt-hour to a token for one accelerator, using today's rental ask. Compute the break-even tokens per second for two models and compare with your bound from day 6.

Write one page, in your own words and with your own numbers, answering: is compute a commodity? Then write half a page designing a clearinghouse for three-year leases, what is margined, against which price, how a default is sold, who loses in what order, and half a page attacking it.

spans.text: By the end of the week you can explain why the router's ranking sends requests to endpoints that cost more, why a futures contract on a rental index does not help a lender value a rack, why nobody in the strategic market hedges the GPU-hour, and what the tenor curve does and does not forecast.
The goal is to test the large claims instead of repeating them.

blocks.text: Days twenty-nine and thirty: choose and scope

spans.text: Take the top item on the shortlist and reduce it to something that can be finished in one further week: one question, one dataset, one chart, one page. Write down what result would be interesting and what result would be dull, before collecting anything. Then collect the first day of data.
If nothing on the list fits, the measurement table in
Chapter 22
is the default. A month of a series nobody else has recorded is a contribution whatever it turns out to show.
A good question shows that you know the structure and asks for the one number you cannot get from public sources. These are drawn from the gaps this guide registers.

rows.text: What share of contracted hours were delivered last quarter, and what does the contract say about the rest? How much prepayment did the last customer pay, and was it credited evenly or against the final year?
What does context length do to your tokens per second per accelerator? What share of your fleet is on contracts shorter than a year? Which formats do you serve, and do customers ask?
What value do you assign the hardware at maturity, and what evidence would let you raise it? What happens, step by step, if the customer stops paying in month eighteen?
How much traffic uses the default ranking? Do you measure cache-hit rates by provider, and would you rank on them?
What is the spread between your three-year cost and your one-month price today, and what was it six months ago? What would you hedge with if you could?
Which input sets your delivery dates this year? How much of your capacity is committed under prepayments, and through when?
What is priced into the weakest build-out borrower, and what would have to happen at the strongest for the spreads to converge?

spans.text: One for each idea the guide depends on. If you can answer all of them aloud without notes, you can read anything in the field.
Units and hardware

items.text: Why is 1 GW not a stable unit of performance across chip generations?
Why do large dies yield worse, and why does memory need advanced packaging?
Why are EUV mirrors a bottleneck even when customers will pay billions?
Why does batching set the economics of inference, and what limits the batch?
Why does a four-bit format roughly halve the hardware cost of a token, and why is it a different grade of product?
Why does an old accelerator lose about a third of its rental value a year, and what usually ends its life?

spans.text: Money

items.text: Why can a profitable company have negative free cash flow?
Why is depreciation not a cash cost this year and still an economic one?
How does a customer commitment make a project financeable?
Why is a prepayment both protection against the customer and equity for the operator?
Why did the largest equipment supplier guarantee buildings and power but not its own chips?
What is the difference between a model, a quote, and a print, and which does a rating agency need?
Why can a lab control the use of compute without owning the data center?

spans.text: Markets

items.text: Why does the router rank on the input price, and why does that matter differently for an agent and a chatbot?
Why is a cached token cheap to reuse and not free to keep, and why can the buyer not verify the count?
Why can adding providers raise the cost of a session?
What is in the silicon spread, and which parts are refining and which are not?
Why is the tenor curve not a forward curve, and what lets you separate expected decline from a payment for credit?
Why does nobody in the strategic market hedge the GPU-hour, and what do they trade instead?
What plays the part of storage in a market for something that cannot be stored?
What must be true of the short-term market before a clearinghouse can replace a prepayment?
What knowledge does a rental index carry that an HBM contract price does not, and why?

spans.text: Macro and judgment

items.text: What is the difference between a Treasury yield and a credit spread?
Why do bond prices fall when yields rise, and why does maturity set the speed of a rate shock?
When does the gap between the interest rate and growth destabilize debt?
What centralizes training, and what might decentralize inference?
Which single assumption matters most to any forecast of concentration?
